points.point: The broadest split is by where memory lives: token-level (external text or records retrieved into the prompt), parametric (weights) and latent (hidden states or KV caches). Almost all agent memory systems are token-level.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Memory in the Age of AI Agents.md
points.evidence: Abstract (p. 1): 'three dominant realizations of agent memory, namely token-level, parametric, and latent memory'; §3 Form (p. 12), with §3.1 Token-level (p. 13), §3.2 Parametric (p. 22), §3.3 Latent (p. 25). The 'almost all are token-level' part is the answers' own framing; I did not find it stated in the survey.

points.point: The same survey splits memory by function: factual memory (facts about the user and world), experiential memory (what the agent learned from doing tasks) and working memory (context within one task).
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Memory in the Age of AI Agents.md
points.evidence: Abstract: 'a finer-grained taxonomy that distinguishes factual, experiential, and working memory'; §4 Functions (p. 31), with §4.1 Factual (p. 32), §4.2 Experiential (p. 36), §4.3 Working (p. 42).

points.point: Memory stream with reflection (Generative Agents): every observation is appended to a natural-language log, retrieval is scored by recency, importance and relevance, and higher-level reflections are periodically synthesised. Nothing is overwritten, so an old and a new fact both stay.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Generative Agents. Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior.md
points.evidence: §1 (p. 2): the memory stream 'records, in natural language, a comprehensive list of the agent's experiences. A memory retrieval model combines relevance, recency, and importance'; reflection 'synthesizes memories into higher-level inferences over time'. That contradictions are left unreconciled is the answers' inference from this design, not a quoted statement.

points.point: Tiered, OS-style memory (MemGPT): a small in-context working context and FIFO queue, plus external recall and archival storage. The LLM itself moves data between them by function calls, and a 'memory pressure' warning lets it save what matters before eviction.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/MemGPT. Towards LLMs as Operating Systems.md
points.evidence: §1 (p. 1): 'MemGPT uses functions to move data between main context and external context (the archival and recall storage databases)'. §2.2 (p. 2): at about 70% of the window the queue manager inserts a 'memory pressure' warning so the LLM can store important information to working context or archival storage.

points.point: MemoryOS replaces the model's judgement with fixed short-, mid- and long-term tiers, promoting and evicting by a heat score.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Memory OS of AI Agent.md
points.evidence: §1 (p. 1): storage is organised 'into short-term, mid-term, and long-term storage units', updated by 'dialogue-chain and heat-based mechanisms'. Memory Updating (p. 3): 'STM-to-MTM updates via dialogue-chain FIFO and MTM-to-LPM updates using a segmented page strategy with heat-based replacement'.

points.point: Extracted fact store (Mem0): an LLM extracts facts from each exchange, retrieves the 10 most similar stored memories, and chooses ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP by tool call. A contradicted fact is deleted at write time.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Mem0. Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory.md
points.evidence: §2.1 (p. 3): the system 'retrieves the top s semantically similar memories', and the LLM selects ADD, UPDATE, 'DELETE for removal of memories contradicted by new information', or NOOP. Experiments used 's = 10 similar memories'.

points.point: Temporal knowledge graph (Zep/Graphiti): facts are edges between entities with validity times on two timelines (when a fact was true and when it was ingested). A contradicting new edge invalidates the old one instead of deleting it, so past states stay answerable.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Zep. A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: §2.1 (p. 2): 'Zep implements a bi-temporal model', with timeline T for events and T′ for ingestion. §2.2.3 (p. 3): four timestamps are tracked (t′created, t′expired, t_valid, t_invalid), and 'The introduction of new edges can invalidate existing edges', with an LLM detecting contradictions.

points.point: Linked notes (A-MEM): each memory becomes a note with a description, keywords and tags, is linked to related notes, and can trigger rewrites of existing notes' descriptions ('memory evolution') rather than deletion.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/A-MEM. Agentic Memory for LLM Agents.md
points.evidence: Abstract (p. 1): notes carry 'contextual descriptions, keywords, and tags', links are established to historical memories, and 'memory evolution – as new memories are integrated, they can trigger updates to the contextual representations and attributes of existing historical memories'. 'Deletes nothing' is the answers' inference; the grepped passages describe only updates.

points.point: Typed stores: MIRIX keeps six memory types (Core, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource, Knowledge Vault) under a multi-agent framework. Memanto uses thirteen typed categories over plain vector search and argues knowledge graphs are unnecessary.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/MIRIX. Multi-Agent Memory System for LLM-Based Agents.md
points.evidence: MIRIX abstract (p. 1): 'six distinct, carefully structured memory types: Core, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource Memory, and Knowledge Vault, coupled with a multi-agent framework'. Memanto abstract and §I-A (p. 2): it 'challenges the prevailing assumption that knowledge graph complexity is necessary', with 'thirteen predefined memory categories' and a vector-based architecture 'without reliance on knowledge graphs'.

points.point: Experience (procedural) memory stores how to do tasks, not facts about the user. Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable workflows from past trajectories, offline or online.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Agent Workflow Memory.md
points.evidence: Abstract (p. 1): 'a method for inducing commonly reused routines, i.e., workflows, and selectively providing workflows to the agent', applying 'to both offline and online scenarios'.

points.point: ReasoningBank distils up to three strategy items per finished task, from failed as well as successful trajectories.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/ReasoningBank. Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory.md
points.evidence: Abstract and §1 (p. 1): it distils strategies 'from both successful and failed experiences'. Appendix, Memory Extraction (p. 21): 'For each trajectory, at most 3 memory items could be extracted… from both successful and failed trajectories'. The limit is on p. 21, not p. 4 as one answer links. The append-only claim was not checked.

points.point: Who controls writes is a separate axis: a fixed pipeline or rules (Mem0, Zep), the LLM itself through tool calls (MemGPT), or a policy trained with RL. Memory-R1 learns ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP with RL from only 152 training QA pairs.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Memory-R1. Enhancing Large Language Model Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement.md
points.evidence: Abstract (p. 1): agents 'fine-tuned with outcome-driven RL (PPO and GRPO)… With only 152 training QA pairs, Memory-R1 outperforms strong baselines'; the operations are ADD, UPDATE, DELETE and NOOP. The three-way grouping is the answers' synthesis; I did not confirm the heuristic/prompted/learned wording in the Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents survey.

points.point: In Mem-α the RL training, not the memory design, gives the gain: the same framework scores 0.389 with the untrained base model and 0.642 after training.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Mem-α. Learning Memory Construction via Reinforcement Learning.md
points.evidence: §4.3 (p. 7), Table 3: 'The base Qwen3-4B model achieves only 0.389 average performance—substantially below both RAG-Top2 (0.567) and Long-Context (0.588)'; the trained row is 0.642.

points.point: When the work is done differs: Mem0 and Zep pay at write time, long context pays at read time, and LightMem moves consolidation to an offline 'sleep-time' update.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/LightMem. Lightweight and Efficient Memory-Augmented Generation.md
points.evidence: Abstract (p. 1): 'long-term memory with sleep-time update employs an offline procedure that decouples consolidation from online inference'. §1 (p. 1): new entries are first stored with timestamps as 'soft' updates and reconciled later offline. The write-time/read-time contrast for Mem0, Zep and long context is the answers' framing.

points.point: Unit of storage: SeCom finds topical segments are a better memory unit than turns, sessions or summaries.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/On Memory Construction and Retrieval for Personalized Conversational Agents.md
points.evidence: Abstract (p. 1): 'The granularity of memory unit matters: Turn-level, session-level, and summarization-based methods each exhibit limitations'; the paper proposes segment-level memory. I did not check the Table 1 numbers (p. 6).

points.point: No architecture wins everywhere. In a study of 12 systems, composite hybrids lead conversational QA, and graph methods excel at single-hop recall but struggle with temporal reasoning. Zep leads LongMemEval, MemOS leads LoCoMo exact match, and long context leads the database workload.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System.md
points.evidence: §1 (p. 1), finding 1: 'No single memory architecture dominates all scenarios. Composite hybrid systems lead on conversational QA, while graph-based methods excel in single-hop factual recall but struggle with temporal reasoning.' §4.1 (p. 7): Zep reaches 48.0 LLM-judge accuracy on LongMemEval, MemOS 11.5 EM on LoCoMo, and Long Context 48.20 EM on DB-Bench (MemoChat has the higher task success rate there, 55.40).

points.point: Structure is costly: Zep and Cognee reach the top utility only at about 155 s and 117 s of amortised latency per query, against 3.7 s for LightMem. The cost driver is how widely each write propagates, not whether there is a graph, and local maintenance is cheaper than global reorganisation.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System.md
points.evidence: §4.5 (p. 10), O7: LightMem reaches 48.3 normalised utility at 3.67 s; 'Cognee and Zep exceed 84 utility only after 116.5 s and 155.1 s'; 'operational efficiency is governed less by whether a system uses structure than by how widely each write propagates'. Abstract: 'localized maintenance is more cost-efficient than global reorganization'.

points.point: In the same cost comparison, Mem0 scores 21.4 normalised utility at 35.9 s.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System.md
points.evidence: §4.5 (p. 10): LightMem and MemTree 'are clearly more efficient than MemoChat (28.0 at 15.4 s), Mem0 (21.4 at 35.9 s), and A-MEM (57.7 at 17.9 s)'.

points.point: Every abstraction layer (compression, summarisation, fact extraction) discards information, and consolidation often destroys chronological cues, so raw long context still beats most memory systems on time-dependent queries.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System.md
points.evidence: §1 (p. 1), finding 4: 'For time-dependent queries, raw long-context retrieval still outperforms most memory-backed approaches, indicating that standard semantic consolidation often destroys crucial chronological cues.' Finding 6: 'Each layer of abstraction (e.g., compression, summarization, and fact extraction) progressively discards information.'

points.point: Raw text beats summaries as the stored value: storing raw user turns scores 26.0 against 11.7 for summaries in an ablation. LongMemEval also finds that compressing sessions into summaries or facts loses information.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System.md
points.evidence: §5.1 (p. 11), Table 3: LightMem User-Only Raw 26.0 against User-Only Summary 11.7, LongMemEval substring EM; 'Retaining the original conversational content is more important than increasing abstraction or hierarchy'. LongMemEval, CP 1: Value (p. 7): 'compressing sessions into summaries or user-specific facts… can lead to information loss'.

points.point: Graph systems handle knowledge updates best: Zep scores 44.4 on LongMemEval knowledge-update questions against 15.6 for Mem0 and 20.0 for long context, with Mem0 and Letta below long context. Fact-extraction and append-only stores struggle with targeted overwrites and return stale facts.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System.md
points.evidence: §4.3 (p. 9), Table 2, Knowledge Update substring EM: Zep 44.4, Long Context 20.0, Mem0 15.6, Letta (MemGPT) 17.8. §1 finding 3: 'Graph-based methods handle knowledge updates most reliably, whereas popular fact-extraction plugins and append-only stores struggle with targeted overwrites.'

points.point: Full context beats Mem0 in Mem0's own paper on LoCoMo (72.90 against 66.88 LLM-judge score). Mem0's advantage is latency: p95 of 1.44 s against 17.12 s.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Mem0. Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory.md
points.evidence: Table 2 (under the §4.2 heading, p. 10; linked as p. 11 by the answers): full context 72.90 ± 0.19% with p95 17.117 s; Mem0 66.88 ± 0.15% with p95 1.440 s. §4.3: 'around 1.44 seconds (a 92% reduction)… the full-context approach can provide a slight accuracy edge'.

points.point: Store size differs greatly: Mem0 keeps about 7K tokens per LoCoMo conversation and Zep's graph more than 600K, and Zep's new memories became usable only after hours. This is Mem0's own measurement of a competitor.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Mem0. Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory.md
points.evidence: §4.5: Mem0 'occupies only 7k tokens per conversation on an average… Zep's memory graph consumes in excess of 600k tokens'; 're-running identical searches after a delay of several hours yielded considerably better results'. The heading's page is cut off in my output; the answers cite p. 14.

points.point: Memory wins once the history is long: on LongMemEval's roughly 115K-token histories, Zep scores 71.2% against 60.2% for full context with gpt-4o, using about 1.6K prompt tokens. The result is vendor-run.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Zep. A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: §4.3.2 (p. 7), Table 2: Full-context gpt-4o 60.2% at 115k tokens; Zep gpt-4o 71.2% at 1.6k tokens. With gpt-4o-mini the scores are 55.4% and 63.8%.

points.point: Long context is still a strong baseline across 15 memory methods in EvoMemBench: Gemini-3-Flash on raw context scores 83.0 on the LongMemEval subset against at most 52.0 for any memory method.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/benchmarks/EvoMemBench. Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective.md
points.evidence: Abstract: '15 representative memory methods… long-context baselines remain highly competitive'. §5.2.1 (p. 6), Table 3, LME (S*) column: Gemini-3-Flash 83.00; the best memory method is Mem0 at 52.00 (A-MEM 51.00, BM25 50.33). Finding 1 (p. 6) says the same.

points.point: Memory methods are better at retaining than revising: on multi-hop questions over updated facts (FactConsolidation), every memory method scores 7% or less in EvoMemBench.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/benchmarks/EvoMemBench. Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective.md
points.evidence: §5.2.1 (p. 6), Table 3, FC MH column: BM25 7.00, Mem0 7.00, A-MEM 5.00, GraphRAG 4.00, MemOS 3.00, MemAgent 3.00, MemoryOS 2.00, MemoBrain 1.00; Gemini-3-Flash on long context scores 58.00. Finding 2 (p. 6): 'Existing memory methods are better at retention than revision.'

points.point: On MemoryAgentBench, simple baselines beat commercial memory systems: long-context GPT-5-mini scores 60.6 overall and BM25 41.5, against 21.1 for Mem0, 24.0 for Zep and 28.3 for MemGPT. The memory systems ran on the weaker GPT-4o-mini.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/benchmarks/Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions.md
points.evidence: Table 3 (under the §4.1 heading, p. 7; the answers cite p. 8), overall column: GPT-5-mini (400K) 60.6, BM25 41.5, HippoRAG-v2 41.6, Mem0 21.1, Zep 24.0, MemGPT 28.3. Caption: 'All RAG agents and commercial memory agents use GPT-4o-mini as the backbone'; long-context GPT-4o-mini scores 42.2. HippoRAG-v2 at 41.6 is marginally above BM25.

points.point: Forgetting is a separate capability from recall. In ForgetEval a verbatim store scores 40% on a recall benchmark and 0 of 385 on adversarial deletion. An LLM at write time fixes canonicalisation but not intent-aware deletion, and an LLM at mutation time fixes the reverse.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting. An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen.md
points.evidence: §1 (p. 1): 'MemPalace saturates the recall plane (60/150 on Memora) yet fails every control-plane test (0/385 on adversarial forgetting)'. §5.7 (p. 8): 'Inscribe-time LLM… recovers canonicalization (… 100 %) but cannot help prefix_collision or compound_fact (0 %)… Mutation-time LLM (our hook) recovers those (compound_fact 78–85 %, prefix_collision 79 %)'.

points.point: Graph systems nearly fail targeted deletion: Graphiti (Zep's engine) passes 7.0% of the adversarial cases it could be scored on, HippoRAG 9.5%, and Mem0 with LLM extraction 43.6%. The study is single-author, from the builder of one tested system (Lethe).
points.paper: library/llm/memory/agent/Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting. An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen.md
points.evidence: Limitations (p. 9): 'Graphiti scores 17/242 evaluable (7.0 %) with 143 cases N/A'; 'HippoRAG scores 31/326 evaluable (9.5 %)… strict-denominator 31/385 = 8.0 %'; Mem0 infer=True '168/385 = 43.6 %', against 68.3% with infer off (Appendix P). The sole author is Dongxu Yang, affiliation DeepLethe. These numbers are in Limitations and the appendices, not on p. 8.

points.point: Most loss happens at write time: in HaluMem every system except MemOS recalls under 60% of the memory points it should have extracted. The benchmark's authors include the company behind MemOS.
points.paper: library/llm/memory/benchmarks/HaluMem. Evaluating Hallucinations in Memory Systems of Agents.md
points.evidence: §6.2.1 (p. 11): 'In the memory extraction task, regarding memory integrity, except for MemOS, all systems achieve recall (R) rates below 60%, indicating that many reference memory points are not extracted.' Affiliations include MemTensor (Shanghai) Technology, with corresponding author lizy@memtensor.cn.

noreviews+claude-sonnet-5-5-q4-r1.comment: A catalogue built from the index summaries, which it states ("I'm working from the index summaries, not from full reads of the papers"). The one-line descriptions I checked match the papers: MIRIX's six managers, Memanto's thirteen categories, the six operations in Rethinking Memory, Memory-R1's 152 pairs, and the folder counts 70/18/10. Points 3, 4, 7, 10 and 14 are made only in part (no append-only log, function calls, edge invalidation, or write-time versus read-time contrast). It gives no comparative evidence and no page numbers, so it says what kinds exist but little on how they differ in practice. "Tests 13 systems" is loose: the paper compares thirteen system configurations.

errors.quote: Tiered context (OS-style) | ... | The agent itself edits the in-prompt block through a function call | MemGPT, MemoryOS, LightMem
errors.paper_says: This holds for MemGPT only. MemoryOS moves content between fixed short-, mid- and long-term tiers by FIFO and a heat score, not by the agent's function calls (Memory OS of AI Agent, §3.2–3.3, p. 3–4). In Are We Ready (§3.4, p. 6) LightMem is described as an append-only insert of timestamped facts.

noreviews-q4-r3.review_only: This rests on the library's notes for about 25 of the 70 memory papers; for the rest (marked * below) I used only the index summaries, not the papers.
noreviews-q4-r3.comment: The widest coverage of the graded points, and every number I checked is in the paper: 0.389/0.642, 155/117/3.7 s, 72.90/66.88, 83.0/52.0, 7% or less, 7.0%/9.5%/43.6% (Control-Plane, p. 9). The LoCoMo label permutation is real: A-MEM's 27.02 / 45.85 / 12.14 / 44.65 sit under Multi Hop / Temporal / Open Domain / Single Hop in A-MEM (p. 6) and under Single Hop / Temporal / Multi-Hop / Open Domain in Mem0 (p. 9). The Are We Ready tie to MemOS also holds (shared authors Zhiyu Li and Feiyu Xiong). "On tool-use execution, procedural memory is best" holds for the in-episode setting (EvoMemBench Finding 4, p. 7) but not cross-episode, where retrieval-augmented memory ranks best on Tool Using (Finding 7, p. 8). Points 5 and 7 are made only in part. I could not confirm from the markdown that Fig. 7 of Are We Ready and Table 2 of Mem0 are on the pages it cites.

errors.quote: Nearly all agent memory systems are the text kind, because only text can be shown to a user, deleted on request and used with any model (Memory in the Age of AI Agents, p. 12)
errors.paper_says: The survey says token-level memory is "the most common memory form" and "typically transparent, easy to edit, and straightforward to interpret" (§3.1, p. 13), and that it is often plug-and-play (p. 30). It does not give these as the reason for its prevalence and does not say only text has them; p. 12 holds just the three-form definition.

errors.quote: Experience (ExpeL, Agent Workflow Memory, ReasoningBank) | ... | A wrong lesson keeps being applied; nothing prunes.
errors.paper_says: ExpeL prunes: insights can be DOWNVOTEd, and "if an insight's importance count reaches zero, it will be removed" (ExpeL, p. 4).

errors.quote: Extract-and-consolidate (Mem0, A-MEM, LightMem) | An LLM extracts the fact, fetches the 10 most similar stored facts and chooses add, update, delete or nothing.
errors.paper_says: This is Mem0's procedure (s = 10, Mem0 §2.1, p. 3). A-MEM builds notes, links them and rewrites neighbours' descriptions (A-MEM §3.1–3.3, p. 4); it has no delete operation.

asis-q4-r1.review_only: Everything else above that carries no page link rests on the review alone.
asis-q4-r1.misleading: Slightly. Under "Graphs are not a general accuracy upgrade" it rests on AgentMemBench's 0.001 graph Recall@5 with no caveat that this is an NER entity graph run with a 4-bit 7B model on 491 questions, and it omits the larger study's finding that graph systems lead on knowledge updates and single-hop recall.
asis-q4-r1.comment: The numbers with page links all check out: 7K/600K tokens (Mem0, p. 14), 72.90/66.88 and 17.12/1.44 s, Zep 71.2% against 60.2% at 1.6K tokens (p. 7, Table 2), AgentMemBench 0.573/0.001/0.005 (p. 10), Cartridges 38.6× (p. 1). The MemoryLLM correction is right: the paper says the model "retains knowledge even after 20 updates" (p. 7), and N/K = 7680/256 = 30. It uses none of the head-to-head studies behind points 16–21 and 25–30. It also says outright that the Zep-versus-Mem0 ranking claim is from the review and was not rechecked. Points 4 and 7 are made only in part.

errors.quote: Flat extract-and-retrieve | Short facts pulled out by an LLM, embedded in a vector store | ... | Mem0, SeCom, LightMem
errors.paper_says: SeCom does not extract facts. It partitions conversations into topical segments and concatenates the retrieved segments, "bypassing summarization to avoid the information loss" (On Memory Construction and Retrieval, p. 1).

errors.quote: AgentMemBench claims a plain key-value store beats graphs and summaries on every axis (p. 1)
errors.paper_says: The paper says "EKV dominates on every quality axis" (p. 1, p. 10). On footprint it is the worst: 5,126 tokens against about 300 for windowing and 3,478 for summaries (p. 11).

nonotes-q4-r3.comment: The best-sourced answer: every section and page link I checked points to the right heading, and the head-to-head findings match the papers. These include 12 systems and 11 datasets, 155/117/3.7 s, Mem0 21.4 at 35.9 s (Are We Ready, p. 10), 40% and 0/385 (Control-Plane, §5.5, p. 6), the write-time versus mutation-time result (§5.7, p. 8), and MemoryArena 40–60% (Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents, p. 4, Table 1). "The 2023 systems were designed for 8k-token contexts" is supported only for MemGPT (GPT-4 at 8,192 tokens, p. 4); Generative Agents and MemoryBank do not state it. Points 1, 6, 9, 21 and 25 are made without their numbers or full detail. It leaves out the vendor-paper results (points 22–24) and the write-time loss and revision results (points 26, 30).

asis-q4-r3.review_only: The numbers below are checked against the paper notes.
asis-q4-r3.comment: Every number I checked matches the papers: Mem0 Table 2 (72.90 vs 66.88, p95 1.440 s vs 17.117 s), Mem0 §4.5 p. 14 (7k vs 600k tokens), Zep Table 2 p. 7 (71.2% vs 60.2%, 1.6k vs 115k), MemoryAgentBench Table 3 (60.6 / 21.1 / 24.0 / 28.3, memory agents on GPT-4o-mini), HaluMem p. 11 (all but MemOS under 60% recall). Only 4 papers carry page links (Mem0, Zep, MemoryAgentBench, HaluMem); the other 19 are named in the family table. Points 3, 4 and 5 are only gestured at ('everything is kept', 'the model itself', 'a usage score'), so not counted; point 12 is counted for the axis, without the Memory-R1 figure. It misses the functional split, the independent 12-system study (points 16-21), forgetting (28-29) and EvoMemBench. Not checked: 'eight families' and the 'same system moves by more than the claimed margins' claim, which come from the review.

errors.quote: Rethinking Memory in LLM-based Agents for the write/manage/read loop
errors.paper_says: The write–manage–read loop is from 'Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers' (abstract and Contributions: 'We formalize agent memory as a write–manage–read loop'). 'Rethinking Memory in LLM based Agents' never uses the phrase; it organises memory into parametric and contextual forms and six atomic operations.

errors.quote: Both put 1–3K tokens in the prompt.
errors.paper_says: Minor. In Mem0's Table 2, the same paper that gives the 7K and 600K store sizes, Zep's retrieved context is 3,911 tokens and Mem0's is 1,764. Zep is in the 1–3K range only in its own LongMemEval run (1.6k, Zep Table 2, p. 7).

asis+claude-sonnet-5-5-q4-r1.review_only: I took this from the review alone and didn't open the individual papers, so treat the numbers as the review's.
asis+claude-sonnet-5-5-q4-r1.misleading: Mildly. It files A-MEM, LightMem and SeCom under 'one memory is an LLM-extracted fact', although SeCom stores topical segments and A-MEM linked notes. 'Graphs aren't a good default' leans on AgentMemBench, whose graph strategy is a spaCy triple extractor (p. 6), not Zep or HippoRAG. It gives no page references, so nothing can be looked up.
asis+claude-sonnet-5-5-q4-r1.comment: No page citations or links; 33 papers are named, none located. The numbers it does give hold: 7K vs 600K (Mem0 p. 14), 44.4 vs 15.6 (Are We Ready Table 2), 7–9.5% (ForgetEval Limitations and Appendix N), under 60% recall (HaluMem p. 11), and AgentMemBench graph Recall@5 of 0.001 on LoCoMo (p. 10). The five design questions are a useful frame and cover point 12 and point 14 (including LightMem's idle-time work). No mechanism is explained beyond one table cell, and it ends by offering to do the checking it did not do.

errors.quote: Experiential memory is best on tool-use execution
errors.paper_says: True only within an episode. EvoMemBench Finding 4 (p. 7) has procedural methods (ReasoningBank, AWM) strongest on in-episode execution. Finding 7 (p. 8), in the cited range, says that across episodes 'In Tool Using, retrieval-augmented memory achieves the best family-level average rank' (5.43); procedural memory is best only in Embodied AI.

errors.quote: ReasoningBank distils up to three strategy items per finished task ... ([ReasoningBank, p. 4]
errors.paper_says: Minor page error. §3.2 on p. 4 says only 'we extract multiple memory items for each trajectory' and defers to Appendix A.1; the limit ('at most three memory items') is in Appendix A.1, p. 21. The failures-and-successes and append-only parts are on p. 4.

noreviews-q4-r1.review_only: I worked from the library's notes on 17 of the 42 agent papers and 5 of the 10 benchmarks; the rest, including MemOS, MIRIX, HippoRAG, ExpeL and Agent Workflow Memory, are placed by their one-line index summaries only.
noreviews-q4-r1.comment: The strongest answer: it explains mechanisms with a running example and is the only one to use the independent 12-system study. 11 papers carry page links, and they check out: MemGPT memory pressure (§2.2, p. 2), MemoryOS heat (p. 4–5), Generative Agents (p. 8–9), SeCom Table 1 (p. 6), Mem0 (p. 3–4, Table 2), Zep §2.2.3 (four timestamps on two timelines, p. 3), Are We Ready Table 3 (26.0 vs 11.7), Table 2 (Zep 44.4; Mem0 15.6 and Letta 17.8 below long context 20.0) and p. 10 (155.1 s, 116.5 s, 3.67 s), ForgetEval 17/242 = 7.0% (p. 9), MemoryAgentBench BM25 41.5. The counts of 42 agent papers and 10 benchmarks are right, and both HaluMem and Are We Ready do have MemTensor authors. Point 10 is counted for the 'how to do things, not facts about the user' statement; AWM itself is only listed. Point 22 is counted without the latency half. Not checked: that Mem0 and MemoryOS permute LoCoMo category labels, that re-runs of A-MEM and Mem0 come out much lower, and the reference to 'your own note on Zep'. It omits write-time loss (HaluMem), the store-size comparison and Zep's LongMemEval win over full context.

asis-q4-r2.review_only: that comparison rests on the review only, since I did not open those two tables.
asis-q4-r2.comment: Every number I checked matches: Mem0 p. 14 and Table 2, Zep Table 2, Are We Ready Table 2 (44.4 / 15.6 / 20.0), ForgetEval (7.0% and 9.5%, single author), HaluMem p. 11, and Fundamental Problems Table 4 (Generative Accuracy on downstream facts 0.97 before and 0.01 after the edit, §6.5). 7 papers carry page links. The one claim it flags as review-only also holds in the papers, roughly: MemOS's LoCoMo table has Zep 59.22 vs Mem0 64.57 (5.4 below, stated as 6), and MIRIX's has Zep 79.09 vs Mem0 62.47 (16.6 above). 'The corresponding author' of HaluMem is loose: there are two, one at Harbin Engineering University and one at MemTensor. The Memory in the Age citation (p. 29–31) supports text being inspectable and editable, not the hosted-API point. It also opens with 'checked the numbers below against the paper notes'. The bullet headed 'Cost moves between write time and read time' is really about store size, so point 14 is not counted. Points 4 and 5 are only gestured at; point 12 appears as a family, not an axis. It misses the functional split and most of the 12-system study.

errors.quote: ForgetEval shows a system can saturate recall and fail every deletion test
errors.paper_says: The system that fails every deletion case (MemPalace, 0/385) scores 60/150 = 40% on the recall-heavy Memora benchmark, below LangGraph's 45%, so it does not saturate recall (Control-Plane Placement, §5.5, p. 6, Table 3). The paper's 'saturation band' is the 63–68% forgetting pass rate of other systems. This result is in §5.5–5.6 (p. 6–7), not the cited §5.7, p. 8, which holds only the placement finding.

errors.quote: Tiered ("OS-style") | ... | MemGPT, MemoryOS, LightMem | Depends on the model promoting and evicting correctly
errors.paper_says: MemoryOS does not leave promotion and eviction to the model: segments move between tiers by a computed heat score and thresholds (Memory OS of AI Agent, §3.3, p. 4–5). Only MemGPT relies on the model's own function calls.

errors.quote: Linked notes / hybrid | Notes that link to each other and get rewritten as new ones arrive | A-MEM, MIRIX, MemOS
errors.paper_says: MIRIX is not a linked-notes design: it keeps six typed memory components (Core, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource, Knowledge Vault), each maintained by its own Memory Manager under a Meta Memory Manager (MIRIX, §1 p. 1–2, §3.1 p. 6, §3.3 p. 8). The description fits A-MEM only; MemOS was not checked.

nonotes-q4-r2.misleading: Mildly. The six-family table and the comparison findings are sound, but a reader would take MemoryOS to rely on model judgement, MIRIX to be a linked-notes system, and typed stores not to exist as a family. The forgetting bullet overstates the recall side ('saturate' against 40%).
nonotes-q4-r2.comment: Good coverage of the qualitative comparison findings (16, 17, 19, 21, 28), and the only answer giving the cost numbers (116–155 s against 3.7 s, which match p. 10). It has almost no numbers otherwise, and only 4 of the 29 named papers carry a page link. It says openly that per-system descriptions and the EvoMemBench point come from index summaries, not the papers. The 42-paper count, the AgentMemBench caveats (spaCy graph, Qwen2.5-7B generator, p. 10 Table 5) and the finding numbers 3, 4 and 6 all check out. It does not state the MemoryOS heat score (5), typed stores (9) or the ReasoningBank detail (11).

errors.quote: **Parametric** | The weights themselves | MEMIT, Titans, sparse memory finetuning, Text-to-LoRA
errors.paper_says: The survey whose split this table presents puts Titans under latent memory, not parametric: such works 'rely on parameterized modules' but 'their operational memory units remain latent representations, placing them firmly within this category' (Memory in the Age of AI Agents, §3.3.1, p. 26, and Table 3).

errors.quote: Graphiti passes 7% of the cases it could be scored on ([Control-Plane Placement, p. 8]
errors.paper_says: The number is right (17/242 evaluable, 7.0%) but it is stated in the Limitations section, p. 9, and Appendix N. Page 8 (§5.7, Fig. 2) gives only the per-category rates for the KG-abstraction regime.

errors.quote: LightMem only inserts online and reconciles in a "sleep-time" pass, arguing online updates wrongly delete non-conflicting facts ([p. 5]
errors.paper_says: The mechanism is on p. 5 (§3.3), but the argument that an LLM may misread related facts as a conflict and delete the older entry is in §5.6, p. 9. On p. 5 the stated motivation is latency.

noreviews-q4-r2.review_only: about 30 have notes with page-level digests, and systems I cite without a page come from the index one-liners only
noreviews-q4-r2.comment: The most complete and best-supported answer: 21 points, 16 papers with page links, and every number I checked is right. That covers Mem-α 0.389 against 0.642 (p. 7, Table 3), BM25 41.5 with Mem0, Zep and MemGPT at 21.1, 24.0 and 28.3, Mem0 72.9 against 66.9, EvoMemBench 7% or less, and the three benchmark leaders in Are We Ready §4.1. The LoCoMo label-permutation claim also holds: A-MEM's 27.02 is 'Multi Hop' in its own table and 'Single Hop' in both Mem0's and MemoryOS's. The errors are one classification that contradicts the cited survey and two citations pointing at the wrong page. Point 20 is made only through the LongMemEval half, and 27 without the long-context 60.6 or the weaker-backbone caveat. It omits cost (17, 18), information loss (19), knowledge-update results (21) and the long-history case for memory (24).

errors.quote: A study of 12 systems finds graph methods strong on single-hop recall but weak on temporal reasoning, and local maintenance cheaper than global reorganisation: [Are We Ready, p. 7, §4.1]
errors.paper_says: Neither finding is in §4.1, p. 7, which reports only which system leads each workload. The single-hop and temporal statement is finding 1 in the introduction (§1), and local against global maintenance is O7 and Finding 5 in §4.5, p. 10.

nonotes-q4-r1.comment: The most accurate description of the families: all of points 3–11 are stated correctly with section-level links that check out, including the heat score, Memanto's thirteen categories and ReasoningBank learning from failures. It is thin on comparisons: no cost numbers, nothing on information loss, knowledge updates, unit of storage or RL-trained writers beyond naming Memory-R1. Two of the four axes it announces (unit stored, when the LLM works) are never developed, so 12, 14 and 15 are not made. Point 28 is made only through the placement half, and the local-maintenance clause of 17 is present without the cost figures. The Mem0 numbers (about 73% against 67%, p95 1.4 s against 17 s) are on p. 13, §4.3 as cited. It discloses which systems come from index summaries only.

errors.quote: HippoRAG passes 9.5% of evaluable forgetting cases and Graphiti (Zep's engine) 7.0% ([ForgetEval, p. 6](...dest=section.5&page=6))
errors.paper_says: Both figures are correct but the page is wrong. They appear only under '## Limitations (p. 9)' ('Graphiti scores 17/242 evaluable (7.0 %)', 'HippoRAG scores 31/326 evaluable (9.5 %)'), with the Graphiti breakdown in Appendix N (p. 19). Section 5.3 on p. 6 reports Lethe, Mem0 and LangGraph only.

asis-v2-q4-r3.review_only: HippoRAG, MIRIX, MemOS, ExpeL and Agent Workflow Memory have no note in `notes/`. Their one-line descriptions above come from the review only; I did not open those papers.
asis-v2-q4-r3.comment: All checked numbers match the papers: Mem0 72.90/66.88 and 1.44 s/17.12 s, 7k vs 600k tokens (§4.5, p. 14), Zep 71.2/60.2 with 1.6k vs 115k tokens, MemoryAgentBench 60.6/41.5/21.1/24.0/28.3, HaluMem recall below 60% except MemOS (p. 11), ReasoningBank 40.5 to 48.8. Point 3 is counted without the reflection step, and point 4 without the memory-pressure warning. Point 10 is counted on the 'lessons, not facts' half; AWM is only named. SeCom is placed in the extract-and-consolidate family, though it segments rather than choosing add/update/delete; not listed as an error because the row describes the family. It has no functional split, no who-writes or when-work-is-done axis, and no 'no architecture wins' finding. Not checked: the claims about notes, and the permuted LoCoMo column labels.

errors.quote: Mem0 stores about 7k tokens per LoCoMo conversation and answers at p95 1.44 s, against 17.12 s for full context ([Mem0, p. 11, Table 2](...dest=table.2&page=11))
errors.paper_says: The latency figures are in Table 2, but the 7k-token store size is not. It is in §4.5 'Memory System Overhead: Token Analysis and Construction Time' (p. 14).

asis-v2-q4-r1.review_only: Sixteen of the papers in these folders have no note yet, including HippoRAG, MemOS, MIRIX, SAGE, ExpeL and Agent Workflow Memory; for those, the mechanism descriptions rest on the review and the abstracts only.
asis-v2-q4-r1.comment: The only answer that states the who-writes axis, the Mem-α training result (0.389 vs 0.642, §4.3, p. 7) and the write-time versus read-time split. Point 12 is counted without the 152 QA pairs, and point 14 without LightMem's sleep-time update. Checked and correct: 70 memory papers in the folders; ForgetEval 7.0%/9.5% on p. 9 (the only answer with the right page); Zep 44.4 vs Mem0 15.6 (Table 2, p. 9); AgentMemBench 0.001 vs 0.573 (p. 10); ReasoningBank 48.8 vs AWM 44.1; ReasoningBank append-only (Appendix A.2, p. 23: 'directly added without additional pruning'); LoCoMo at 26k tokens (Mem0, p. 6). 'Graphs help updates, not recall' leans on AgentMemBench's NER entity graph, which is a narrow basis, but the number is right. Point 23 is not counted because Zep's 600k is missing. Not checked: the sixteen-notes count and the permuted column labels.

errors.quote: Graph stores pass only 7–9.5% of deletion cases ([ForgetEval, p. 8](...page=8))
errors.paper_says: The 7.0% (Graphiti) and 9.5% (HippoRAG) aggregates are stated under '## Limitations (p. 9)', and Graphiti's again in Appendix N (p. 19). Page 8 (§5.7) has only the per-category Figure 2, which points to Limitations for the totals.

errors.quote: Cartridges matches in-context quality with 38.6× less memory, at about 30 minutes of training per corpus ([Cartridges, p. 1](...page=1))
errors.paper_says: 38.6× is in the abstract (p. 1), but the '~30 minutes on a single 8×H100 node' figure appears only in the closing limitations paragraph, well after the introduction, not on p. 1.

asis-v2-q4-r2.review_only: The numbers above come from the papers' notes, or from the paper itself for AgentMemBench, which has no note. The table rows for HippoRAG, MIRIX, MemOS, Mem-α, SAGE, ExpeL and Agent Workflow Memory rest on the review alone.
asis-v2-q4-r2.comment: Checked and correct: Mem0 table figures; HaluMem below 60% except MemOS (p. 11); raw 26.0 vs summary 11.7 (Table 3, p. 11); Zep 44.4 / Mem0 15.6 / long context 20.0 (Table 2, p. 9); 600K vs 7K (p. 14); AgentMemBench graph 0.001, summarisation 0.005, vector store 0.573 (p. 10); MemoryLLM 1/e after N/K = 30 updates for the main 30×256 model (§3.1.3, p. 3); 'no single system dominates' (§4.1, p. 7). Both HaluMem and Are We Ready do list MemTensor authors, and MemOS is MemTensor's. 'LoCoMo averages about 9K tokens' matches the figure quoted in A-MEM and SeCom, but Mem0's own paper gives 26,000 tokens for the conversations it evaluates, so 'fits in context' holds while the size is understated for the vendor runs. It is the only answer to mention reflections for point 3. Points 4 and 5 are not counted: the OS row lists 'the model, a usage score, a scheduler or agents' without saying which system does which. Not checked: 'single runs with no variance reported' for ReasoningBank, and the note-based claims.
